title: What Are T Levels, and What Is Digital Software Development?
text: What Are T Levels, and What Is Digital Software Development? Digital Software Development T Level → Overview T Levels are two year, Level 3 technical study programmes for 16 19 year olds, sitting alongside A Levels and Apprenticeships as one of the main post 16 routes in England. This page explains what a T Level is in general, and what the T Level Technical Qualification in Digital Software Development (Level 3) covers specifically. T Levels combine classroom theory with a minimum 315 hour industry placement. T Levels as a qualification type T Levels combine: Classroom based theory and practical learning , delivered through a Technical Qualification (TQ). A minimum of 315 hours of industry placement with an employer, giving students real workplace experience. T Level programmes are developed with employers so the content matches what industry actually needs, preparing students for skilled work, an Apprenticeship, or higher level study, including university. The Technical Qualification (TQ) The Technical Qualification is the classroom based, examined half of the T Level, awarded by Pearson. It is built from Outline Content produced by T Level employer, professional body and Provider panels, based on the relevant Apprenticeship Standards. Pearson elaborates that Outline Content into a full specification that: gives Providers (schools/colleges) an accurate, teachable interpretation of what must be covered and assessed; is designed to let students reach threshold competence in the Occupational Specialism; integrates English, maths and digital competencies directly into the taught content (see Competency Frameworks) these are signposted against the Occupational Specialism content using codes like E1, M1 and D1, because that's where students get the most natural opportunity to develop them. What "Digital Software Development" covers This T Level replaces the earlier T Level Technical Qualification in Digital Production, Design and Development . It is aimed at students who want a career building software: coding, problem solving, and creating digital solutions. Unlike some T Levels, it has only one Occupational Specialism (rather than a choice of several) Digital Software Development itself. Students study a shared Core Component covering problem solving, introduction to programming, legislation and regulatory requirements, business context, data, digital environments, security and emerging issues, then go deeper into the Digital Software Development specialism. Qualification purpose The purpose of the qualification is to give students the knowledge and skills to progress into highly skilled employment, an Apprenticeship, or higher level study (including university) in digital software development. By the end, students should have reached threshold competence : they hold the core knowledge and skills for the sector and specialism, and are ready to build toward full occupational competence with further support once they're in a job. Key terms T Level a two year Level 3 technical study programme combining a Technical Qualification with an industry placement. Technical Qualification (TQ) the classroom taught, examined component of a T Level. Outline Content the employer panel defined content framework (based on Apprenticeship Standards) that Pearson turns into the full specification. Threshold competence having the core knowledge and skills needed to be ready to develop full occupational competence on the job, rather than being fully competent from day one. Occupational Specialism the specific occupational pathway a student specialises in during their TQ. This T Level has only one: Digital Software Development. Industry placement the minimum 315 hour employer placement that runs alongside the Technical Qualification. title: Qualification Structure and Assessment
text: Qualification Structure and Assessment Digital Software Development T Level → Overview → Qualification Structure This page covers the qualification summary table, entry requirements, and how the two mandatory components (Core and Occupational Specialism) are assessed. Qualification summary Qualification title T Level Technical Qualification in Digital Software Development (Level 3) Qualification number (QN) 610/5801/4 First teaching September 2025 This qualification replaces 603/5832/4 T Level Technical Qualification in Digital Production, Design and Development Total Guided Learning Hours (GLH) 1260 hours (630 hours core) Total Qualification Time (TQT) 1740 hours (840 hours core) Occupational Specialism(s) Digital Software Development (630 GLH, 900 TQT) there is only one Recommended age range 16 19 Components and weighting Core Paper 1 = 30% of core (15% of total) Core Paper 2 = 30% of core (15% of total) Core Employer Set Project (ESP) = 40% of core (20% of total) Core Component = 50% of total Occupational Specialism = 50% of total Grading information Core and Employer Set Project (ESP) components are graded A E or Unclassified. The Occupational Specialism (OS) component is graded Pass, Merit, Distinction or Unclassified. The overall grading is on a scale of Pass, Merit, Distinction, Distinction or Unclassified, awarded by the Institute for Apprenticeships and Technical Education (IfATE). Entry requirements There are no formal prior learning requirements it's the Provider's responsibility to ensure recruited students have a reasonable expectation of success. Students are most likely to succeed with Level 2 qualifications (e.g. 5 GCSEs at grade 4+ including English and maths, or a vocational Tech Award pass at Level 2), though relevant work experience or aptitude shown through diagnostic tests can also demonstrate readiness. Assessment The core and ESP components are externally set and marked by Pearson. The OS component is set by Pearson and externally marked by Pearson. title: Student Progression and Careers
text: Student Progression and Careers Digital Software Development T Level → Overview → Progression and Careers This page covers who this Technical Qualification is designed for, the job roles it leads to, and the routes students can take after completing it. Student profile Students undertaking this Technical Qualification are 16 19 years old and in full time education. The typical student: has a clear idea about the industry sector they want a career in; has an idea of the type of job role they'd like to explore as a career. Career pathways This Technical Qualification aligns to the Level 3 Apprenticeship for Software Development Technicians , so it supports progression straight into entry level software development job opportunities. Job roles it can lead to include: Software Development Technician Junior Developer Junior Web Developer Junior Application Developer Junior Mobile App Developer Junior Games Developer Junior Software Developer Junior Application Support Analyst Junior Programmer Assistant Programmer Automated Test Developer Progression routes Students have three broad options after completing the T Level: 1. Apprenticeship progress to the Level 3 Software Development Technician Apprenticeship (or similar), to develop and gain certification of full occupational competence, or later to a higher level Apprenticeship such as the Level 4 Software Developer standard, depending on skills and experience. 2. Higher education progress to a relevant Higher National Certificate (HNC), Higher National Diploma (HND) or degree programme, for students who don't have access to an Apprenticeship or prefer a more academic route. Students must check entry requirements for each degree programme with the relevant higher education provider. 3. Direct employment move straight into one of the entry level job roles listed above, since the T Level is designed to deliver threshold competence for the sector. Key terms Threshold competence the level of knowledge and skill needed to be workplace ready and continue developing on the job, short of full occupational competence. Level 3 / Level 4 Apprenticeship the natural next step(s) after this T Level, building toward full occupational competence and, eventually, more senior standards like the Level 4 Software Developer Apprenticeship. title: Grading and Results
text: Grading and Results Digital Software Development T Level → Overview → Grading and Results This page covers how the Technical Qualification is graded and awarded, the Uniform Mark Scale, how the overall T Level grade is calculated, and how results reach students and Providers. How the Technical Qualification is graded and awarded Calculation of the Technical Qualification grade The two components are awarded across these grade ranges: Component Available grade range Core (including Core examinations and Employer Set Project) A E and Unclassified Occupational Specialism Distinction, Merit, Pass and Unclassified The Core grade is calculated by aggregating points across each Core assessment to produce the A E grade. If a student's achievement in either component falls below Pearson's minimum standard, they receive an Unclassified (U) result for that component. Awarding the components Grade boundaries are set for each component/sub component (Core Examinations, Employer Set Project, Occupational Specialism) in every assessment series, through a process called awarding . This keeps standards consistent over time, so students get the same opportunity to achieve regardless of which assessment series they sit. Uniform Mark Scale (UMS) For the Core component, students' raw marks are converted to a Uniform Mark Scale. This benchmarks outcomes between different assessment series, so a student who produces a C grade standard response in the Employer Set Project in one series gets the same uniform mark as a student performing at that same standard in a different series, regardless of raw marks. The maximum uniform marks and grade boundaries per sub component are fixed: Grade Core Exam (max 240) Core ESP (max 160) Core Overall (max 400) A 216 240 144 160 360 400 A 192 215 128 143 320 359 B 168 191 112 127 280 319 C 144 167 96 111 240 279 D 120 143 80 95 200 239 E 96 119 64 79 160 199 U 0 95 0 63 0 159 Where the Core component has two Core Exams (Paper 1 and Paper 2), the results are combined before converting to UMS. Calculation of the T Level grade The Department for Education uses a T Level grade look up table with minimum thresholds. Students must: complete both components, achieve at least a grade E in the Core, and achieve at least a Pass in the Occupational Specialism, as well as successfully completing the other elements of the T Level, like the industry placement. Students who don't meet the minimum requirements are not certificated. Results transfer to Providers Technical Qualification result days Assessment series Results day Summer August (Level 3 Results Day) November March (normally the third week, Level 3 Results Day) Pearson issues results directly to Providers and makes available: Scorecards achievement in percentage terms against each Assessment Objective. Results Plus an item by item breakdown so Providers can spot trends across and within cohorts, each labelled with its Assessment Objective. Statement of Provisional Results a provisional component result slip, clearly watermarked as provisional. Pearson doesn't require Providers to complete any forms or processes to claim the Technical Qualification result, since Pearson doesn't issue TQ certificates, T Level certificates, or T Level statements of achievement directly. T Level results reporting The Technical Qualification forms part of the overall T Level. The Department for Education issues T Level results on Level 3 Results Day in August, and provides T Level certificates to students who successfully complete every element of the T Level. Key terms Uniform Mark Scale (UMS) the standardised scale raw marks are converted to, so grades are comparable across different assessment series. Awarding the process of setting grade boundaries each series to keep standards consistent. Unclassified (U) the result given when a student's achievement falls below the minimum standard for a component. Related pages What are T Levels? Qualification structure and assessment Student progression and careers

title: Core Component Overview
text: Core Component Overview Digital Software Development T Level → Core Component The Core Component is the shared foundation every student studies before specialising. It covers the underpinning knowledge and skills that support threshold competence across the digital sector problem solving, programming fundamentals, business context, data, digital environments and security and is assessed through two written exam papers plus an Employer Set Project. The shared core of knowledge that underpins the Digital Software Development specialism. Purpose The Core Component builds the knowledge base that underpins software development work generally: how to break down and solve problems, how to write and reason about code, the business and legal context software is built within, how data is structured and used, the hardware/network/cloud environments code runs in, and the security risks that come with all of it. The Occupational Specialism then goes deep on the practical craft of designing, building, testing and maintaining software itself. The three assessments Part What it covers Weighting (of the core) Core Paper 1 Problem solving · Introduction to programming · Emerging issues · Legislation and regulatory requirements 30% (90 marks, 2h 15m written exam) Core Paper 2 Business context · Data · Digital environments · Security 30% (90 marks, 2h 15m written exam) Employer Set Project A substantial, externally set and marked project (14h 30m) drawing synoptically on the whole core 40% (100 marks) For exact assessment objective breakdowns and exam structure, see Core scheme of assessment. Key terms Threshold competence having the core knowledge and skills needed to be ready to build full occupational competence on the job. Synoptic assessment assessment (here, the Employer Set Project) that draws together knowledge and skills from across the whole core component rather than testing isolated topics. title: Core Paper 1: Problem Solving, Programming, Emerging Issues and Legislation
text: Core Paper 1: Problem Solving, Programming, Emerging Issues and Legislation Digital Software Development T Level → Core Component → Core Paper 1 Core Paper 1 is a 2 hour 15 minute written exam worth 90 marks (30% of the core assessments). It covers four content areas: Problem solving , Introduction to programming , Emerging issues , and Legislation and regulatory requirements . Where the specification says "code", it means Python 3.10 or later. This page follows the specification's own numbering so you can cross reference the official document. Content area 1: Problem solving Students learn to solve digital software development problems, whole solutions or parts of them, expressing solutions as systems, processes, relationships, data organisation or code. 1.1 Computational thinking What it is, when to use it, its benefits/drawbacks, and its four components, each with its own benefits and drawbacks to weigh: Decomposition breaking a problem or solution into smaller, more manageable parts: identify the main features, characterise each one, then split it down. Represented using block diagrams, information flow diagrams, flowcharts, code, or written descriptions. Pattern recognition finding trends and similarities within and between problems/processes, spotting common features between a new problem and existing solutions, and using patterns to make predictions. Abstraction identifying what information is actually needed, filtering out unnecessary detail, and hiding internal workings: working out what inputs are needed, what outputs/outcomes are expected, what varies vs. stays constant, and what key/repeated actions the solution performs. Students should be able to judge how the four components relate to each other and how suitable each is for a given problem. 1.2 Algorithmic design Algorithms and their purpose/characteristics; expressed as flowcharts (terminators, processes, sub processes, decisions, inputs/outputs, arrows, labels), written descriptions (using hierarchical markers to show sequence), or code (see Python and flowchart notation) each with its own benefits and drawbacks. Actions that control the order of steps: sequence , selection , iteration . Students must be able to determine an algorithm's purpose and output, identify and correct errors in one, translate between notations, and design algorithms/solutions that use these actions. 1.3 Strategies Approaches to solving problems: top down , bottom up , modularisation (their purpose, when used, benefits/drawbacks). Root cause analysis approaches: five whys, failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA), event tree analysis (ETA), with follow up actions (log, close, or escalate to a manager/specialist/third party). The high level problem solving strategy: define the problem, gather information, analyse the information, make a plan of action, implement a solution, review the solution. Students should be able to judge which strategy suits a given digital software development problem. Content area 2: Introduction to programming Students analyse problems involving software, people, processes and data, and use tools/techniques to build a complete solution or part of one. 2.1 Standard data types Integer, float, string, Boolean definitions, purpose, and when each is used. 2.2 Variables and constants Definitions and purpose of variables and constants; purpose of data type conversion functions (see Appendix 2); scope and how variables are managed by it (global vs. local). Students must be able to declare and use variables/constants of standard data types, use scope, and use conversion functions. 2.3 Data structures List , array , dictionary purpose and when each is used. Students must be able to interpret, develop and debug code that uses data structures. 2.4 Operators Arithmetic (add, subtract, divide, multiply, exponentiation, integer division, modulus), relational (equivalence, less than, greater than, not equal, less/greater than or equal to), Boolean (not, and, or) see Appendix 2 for the actual operators. Students must be able to use, interpret, create and debug code using operators. 2.5 Input and output Implementing input/output via keyboard, screen, or text file, including the text file cycle: open for reading, open for writing, write lines, close the file. Students must be able to interpret, create and debug code using input/output. 2.6 Actions Sequence , selection (if / else if / else / match case), and loops count controlled and condition controlled, i.e. iteration via count controlled for loops and condition controlled while loops, with their benefits/drawbacks. Students must be able to interpret, develop and debug code using sequence, selection and iteration. 2.7 Functions and procedures Functions may or may not take parameters but must return a result; procedures may or may not take parameters but must not return a result. Both can be user written, pre written/built into the language, pre written in language libraries, or pre written in third party libraries, each with benefits/drawbacks. Students must be able to interpret, develop and debug code using both. 2.8 Validation Presence, length, range, type, format and check digit checks definition and purpose. Students must be able to interpret, develop and debug code using validation. 2.9 Design considerations and programming practices Determining logical order of actions and operations (for accuracy and to avoid errors), choosing data structures and action order for efficient execution time/memory use, naming conventions (meaningful names, camelCase, snake case) and their impact on readability alongside whitespace and line length. Students must judge an algorithm's suitability against requirements, efficiency, appropriateness of data structures/types/variables/constants, presentation and maintainability. 2.10 Robust code Characteristics of robust code: handles unexpected inputs, handles unexpected terminations, produces specific/meaningful error messages. Debugging (locating and correcting errors) and its role in producing robust solutions. Students must be able to locate and correct errors in code. 2.11 Common algorithms Searching : linear search, binary search. Sorting : bubble sort, insertion sort, merge sort. Students need the benefits/drawbacks of each, metrics to compare algorithms (memory use, execution time, number of comparisons), and best/worst/average case reasoning (Big O not required), then must judge which searching/sorting algorithm suits a given situation. 2.12 Testing Why individual components (software, hardware, data, interfaces, the resulting service) are tested before final integration. Testing methods : concept, unit, boundary, integration, performance, system, acceptance, usability, regression, load/stress, closed box, open box purpose, benefits, drawbacks, when used. Automation : macros, scripts, functional testing tools. Test data types : valid, invalid, boundary, erroneous. A test plan 's structure: identify tests, describe their purpose, identify test data, describe expected results, record actual results. Content area 3: Emerging issues 3.1 Impact of digital technologies How increased reliance on digital systems affects organisational culture (communication method changes, productivity/availability expectations, staff monitoring, remote/hybrid working, automation including AI) and society (job loss, shifting skills, less human decision making, privacy, changing behaviours, wider social/online access, potential isolation, improved information access, generative AI, globalisation/access to global media). Digital inclusion : fair access (suitable tech, connectivity, checking dataset bias, best practice codes, public sector accessibility regulations). How end user characteristics (age, digital/literacy skills, internal vs. external audience, cultural issues/bias, additional/accessibility needs) affect inclusivity. Benefits of professional development (competence, employability, standards knowledge). 3.2 Emerging technologies Impact of developments in storage media, processing (quantum computing), the Internet of Things (edge computing; industrial/smart city/domestic use), AI (generative AI, machine learning), extended reality (AR/VR), open source software, blockchain, environmental factors (rare metals, energy to produce systems, disposal impact), and autonomous machines (self driving cars, robotic assembly lines) on organisations, individuals and society. Students must judge the interrelationships and impacts of these technologies in a digital software development context. Content area 4: Legislation and regulatory requirements 4.1 Legislation Health and safety : the Health and Safety at Work Act (safe environment, trained staff, welfare, information/instruction/supervision) and display screen equipment rules (workstation assessments, breaks, eye tests, training) plus the risks of digital work and how to mitigate them (training, safe environment/practices). Data security and protection : the Data Protection Act / UK GDPR, its purpose, and its eight principles. Computer misuse : the Computer Misuse Act (CMA) 1990's principles, consequences for company/employee, employee awareness, and the types of crime it covers. Equality legislation : the nine protected characteristics, types of discrimination (direct, indirect, harassment, victimisation), where individuals are protected, and time limits for claims. Intellectual property : unregistered designs, registered designs, patents. International law : that it applies to some offences, e.g. in cyberspace and surveillance. Students must judge how digital software development interacts with this legislation and its impact on organisations, society and individuals. 4.2 Guidelines Codes of conduct sources: organisational, professional (British Computer Society, The Institution of Analysts and Programmers, Chartered Institute of Information Security), governmental and how they shape professional behaviour (following policy/legislation, minimising public risk, competence/integrity, meeting deadlines, communication, confidentiality/trust). Digital industry standards sources: ISO, WCAG, W3C, IETF, British Standard (BS), IEEE, PCI SSC. Acceptable use policies (AUP) : purpose and typical content (permitted/prohibited activities, working practices, communication etiquette, sanctions). The importance of whistleblowing procedures. Students must judge how guidelines interact with digital software development and their impact on organisations, society and individuals. Key terms Computational thinking the four part approach (decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithmic design) to breaking down and solving problems. Scope the region of a program where a variable is accessible (global or local). Robust code code that handles unexpected inputs/terminations gracefully and gives meaningful errors. Threshold competence having enough knowledge/skill to be ready to build full occupational competence on the job. title: Core Paper 2: Business Context, Data, Digital Environments and Security
text: Core Paper 2: Business Context, Data, Digital Environments and Security Digital Software Development T Level → Core Component → Core Paper 2 Core Paper 2 is a 2 hour 15 minute written exam worth 90 marks (30% of the core assessments). It covers four content areas: Business context , Data , Digital environments , and Security . This page follows the specification's own numbering so you can cross reference the official document. Content area 5: Business context 5.1 Business environment Organisation types by purpose (providing a service or product) and sector: private (SME, large enterprise, NGO), public, voluntary/charity (not for profit). Business models: B2C , B2B , B2M . Stakeholder types: internal (owners, directors, employees) and external (customers/clients, suppliers, shareholders, outsourced services, investors/funders, government). 5.2 Digital value to organisations How digital systems support key organisational areas: sales & marketing (market research, brand promotion/social media, online selling, personalisation, customer retention, analytics), research/design/development (unique products), HR (staff records, performance, training), operations (communication, automation, remote working, document sharing), management (real time KPI monitoring), logistics (automated stock control), and finance (cost reduction, revenue, reporting). How digital systems meet user needs and quality: functionality, reducing "pain points" (response time, task complexity), accessibility, compatibility (legacy/future/external systems), availability, end user support, ease of installation. 5.3 Risk to organisations of using digital systems Potential risks: security breaches (confidentiality/integrity/availability loss), privacy breaches, regulatory/legal non compliance, audience exclusion (bias, poor UX), emerging rival technologies, technical issues (reliance/failure, unfit for purpose). Potential impact: legal action, fines, reputational damage, losing a licence to practise, lost business. 5.4 Technical change management Triggers for change internal (restructuring, expansion, downsizing, new strategic objectives) and external (political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental). How organisations respond : new/amended policies, business processes, products/services, digital systems, training, or restructuring. The change management process : identifying the type of change; the change advisory board's (CAB) role (prioritise/review requests, approval stages, monitor progress, feedback); identifying changes using SMARTER objectives ; identifying impact; allocating resources (budget, time, staffing, hardware/software); communicating risks/impact to stakeholders; configuring the new system; fully testing it; choosing an implementation method (parallel, phased, direct, pilot); documenting the process; rollback planning (backup methodology/location, recovery plan); identifying training needs; monitoring progress; version control software. Feasibility factors : benefits/drawbacks (savings, cost, process impact, reputation), risks (resistance, misuse, inadequate support/knowledge, disruption), and constraints (budget, time, resources). Content area 6: Data Students build fundamental knowledge of data relevant to software development, to communicate with other professionals and to store, access, quality assure, manipulate, analyse and process it. 6.1 Data, information and knowledge The differences and relationships between data, information and knowledge. Sources for generating data: humans (surveys, forms), AI/machine learning (feedback loop dangers), sensors (temperature, accelerometer, vibration, sound, light, pressure), IoT (smart thermostats/lights/cameras/trackers), transactions (customer data, membership, timing, basket). Ethical data practice and metrics for data value: quantity, timeframe, source, veracity. How organisations use data: pattern analysis, system performance analysis, user monitoring, targeted marketing, threat/opportunity assessment. 6.2 Methods of transforming data Manipulating, analysing, processing. 6.3 Data taxonomy Quantitative data is structured ; qualitative data is unstructured . Quantitative data representations: discrete, continuous, categorical values. Qualitative data properties: stored/retrieved only as a single object, or codified into structured data. 6.4 Data types Integer, real, character, string, Boolean, date, Blob definitions, purpose, when used. Students must judge the interrelationships between structured/unstructured data, data type and transformation. 6.5 Data formats JSON, text file, CSV, UTF 8, ASCII, XML definitions, purpose, when used, and their relationship to data transformation. 6.6 Structures for storing data The role of metadata in describing/contextualising data. File based and directory based structures; hierarchy based structures definitions, purpose, when used, and their relationship to data transformation. 6.7 Data dimensions and maintenance The six Vs of Big Data : volume, variety, variability, velocity, veracity, value and their impact on gathering, storing, maintaining and processing data. Data quality assurance methods : validation, verification, reliability, consistency, integrity, redundancy. Factors affecting data maintenance: time, skills, cost. 6.8 Data systems Data wrangling and its steps: structure, clean, validate, enrich, output. A data system's core functions: input, search, save, integrate, organise (index), output, feedback loop. Data entry errors: transcription, transposition and how to avoid them (input validation, double entry verification, drop downs, pre filled boxes). Factors affecting data entry: time/expertise to create screens, time to enter data. 6.9 Data visualisation Formats: graphs, charts, tables, reports, dashboards, infographics benefits/drawbacks based on data type, audience, and brief. 6.10 Data models Hierarchical , network , relational models how they organise data, factors affecting model choice (access efficiency, storage efficiency, implementation complexity), benefits/drawbacks. Students must be able to draw hierarchical/network models (blocks, arrows, labels) and relational models (tables, rows, columns, labels). 6.11 Data access across platforms Permissions (authorisation, privileges, access rights, rules) and access mechanisms: role based access (RBAC), rule based access control (RuBAC), APIs features, purpose, benefits, drawbacks. 6.12 Data analysis tools Storing Big Data for analysis: data warehouse, data lake, data mart. Analysing data: data mining, reporting. Business intelligence use: financial planning/analysis, CRM (customer analytics, communications). Students must judge the relationship between data analysis tools and data scale. Content area 7: Digital environments 7.1 Hardware Physical computer types: personal computers, mobile devices, servers, embedded devices. Hardware device types: input/output devices, processors (cores, clock speed, cache, mobile processors), main memory (RAM/ROM), secondary storage (magnetic/solid state/optical), motherboard, GPUs, network interface devices (PCI, USB), cooling (air/liquid), sensors. 7.2 Software Operating system types: batch, multitasking, real time, network, mobile features and use. Common utilities: file management, defragmenters, file compression, package managers, protection software, backup software. Code development tools: IDEs (editing, debugging, screen design), compilers, interpreters. Common application software: word processors, spreadsheets, databases, email, project management software. 7.3 Networks Benefits/drawbacks of connecting devices into networks. Network types by users/connection/coverage: PAN, LAN, MAN, WAN, VPN. Connectivity: wired (copper/ethernet, fibre optic), wireless (access points). Topologies: star, mesh, tree, and logical vs. physical. Network models: client server, thin client, peer to peer. Common components: server, client, router, switch, internet connection/backbone. The seven layer OSI model (application, presentation, session, transport, network, data link, physical) and the four layer TCP/IP model (application, transport, internet, network), each with their layer functions/protocols. Data packets: contents/structure, role of components, packet switching (packet loss causes), error handling (cyclic redundancy check). Common protocols: web (HTTP/HTTPS), mail (SMTP/POP/IMAP), routing (RIP/OSPF), application (FTP/SFTP/DHCP/DNS). Bandwidth and latency and their effect on performance. 7.4 Virtual environments Components: virtual machines (virtual PC/switch/router clients, servers), hypervisors (type 1/2). Key features: increased security, managed execution, sharing, aggregation, emulation, isolation, portability. Benefits: cost effectiveness at scale, easy management, resilience, lower carbon footprint, better disaster recovery, better testing environments, education/training options. Drawbacks: extra hardware load, slower execution, potential false performance representation. 7.5 Cloud environments Private vs. public cloud. Benefits: portability, elasticity, fewer storage limits, cost effectiveness. Delivery models and how responsibility splits between client and provider: IaaS (client manages apps/software/runtime/data/accounts; provider manages virtualisation/hardware), PaaS (client manages apps/data/accounts; provider also manages systems software/runtime), SaaS (client manages accounts/data only; provider manages everything else). 7.6 Resilient digital environments Benefits: increased security (storage/transfer, fewer vulnerabilities), increased reputation (brand protection, customer confidence), reduced downtime. Methods to improve resilience: software updates/patches, hardware replacement (rolling plans, secure disposal), data/system redundancy, device hardening (removing unneeded ports/apps/permissions/access), backup systems and recovery procedures (onsite, remote/offsite, cloud), hot/cold/warm sites, standard operating procedures (staff training, induction, new systems/policies). Content area 8: Security 8.1 Security risks Confidential information types held by organisations: HR (salaries, personal details), commercially sensitive info (client/stakeholder details, IP, sales figures, contracts), access info (usernames, passwords, MFA details, PINs, access codes, passphrases, biometric data) and why each must stay confidential. Potential impact of failing to maintain privacy/confidentiality: non compliance (losing a licence to practise), lost trust, reputational damage, financial loss (fines, refunds, lost earnings), legal action, reduced security. 8.2 Types of threats and vulnerabilities Technical threats : botnets, DoS/DDoS, malicious hacking (hacktivists/nation states/organised crime/individuals; password cracking/brute force; cross site scripting; SQL injection; buffer overflow), malware (viruses, worms, key loggers, ransomware, spyware, remote access trojans), social engineering (phishing, spear phishing, smishing, vishing, pharming, watering hole attacks, USB baiting), DNS attacks/traffic redirection, insecure APIs, man in the middle attacks, open/unsecured Wi Fi with prevention/mitigation for each. Technical vulnerabilities : inadequate security processes (weak encryption, poor password policy, no MFA), out of date hardware/software/firmware (legacy compatibility, zero day bugs). Human threats : human error, malicious employees, disguised criminals, poor cyber hygiene with prevention/mitigation. Physical vulnerabilities : lack/poor access control, location risks (shoulder surfing, environment, vandalism), poor system robustness, natural disasters with prevention/mitigation. Impact : data loss/leaks, unauthorised access, data corruption, service disruption, unauthorised physical access. 8.3 Threat mitigation Techniques : security settings (hardware/software), anti malware, intrusion detection, encryption (hashing, symmetric, asymmetric), user access policies, staff vetting/training, software based access control, device hardening, backups (full/incremental/differential, safe storage), software/firmware/driver updates, air gaps, API certification, VPNs, MFA, password managers, port scanning, penetration testing (ethical vs. unethical hacking) purpose, process, benefits, drawbacks of each. Internet security processes : firewall configuration (inbound/outbound rules, traffic type, application, IP address), network segregation (virtual, physical, offline), network monitoring, port scanning. 8.4 Interrelationship of components required for effective security The CIA triad : confidentiality (controlling access to keep data private), integrity (ensuring data isn't tampered with, supported by confidentiality), availability (ensuring data is available and useful, supported by integrity) and how they interrelate. The IAAA model : identification (recognising an individual knowledge , possession , or biometric based), authentication (verifying the claimed identity MFA, passwords/passphrases, biometrics), authorisation (ensuring authenticated users only access what they're permitted role based, access control lists), accountability (tracing actions back to a responsible user audit logs, user activity) techniques and their benefits/drawbacks. Key terms CIA triad confidentiality, integrity and availability, the three properties effective security protects. IAAA model identification, authentication, authorisation, accountability. Six Vs of Big Data volume, variety, variability, velocity, veracity, value. CAB (Change Advisory Board) the group that reviews, prioritises and monitors organisational change requests. IaaS / PaaS / SaaS the three cloud delivery models, differing in how much the client vs. the provider manages. title: Employer Set Project
text: Employer Set Project Digital Software Development T Level → Core Component → Employer Set Project The Employer Set Project (ESP) is a substantial, externally set and marked assessment worth 40% of the core assessments (100 marks), taken over a combined duration of up to 14 hours 30 minutes across multiple sessions. It draws synoptically on knowledge and skills from across the whole core component, responding to a realistic vocational brief. Internet access and AI tools are not permitted during the assessed sessions. This page summarises the current specimen assessment material the actual live assessment keeps the same overall number/focus of tasks, but the order and detail of tasks can change each series. Pre task: familiarisation with the industry context Not directly assessed and not taken under controlled conditions. Students investigate the context of the main brief (recent specimen material used the financial sector), working independently and in groups, to inform their responses to the assessed tasks. Task 1: Planning a project Using a Pearson provided template, students produce a project plan containing: A Gantt chart assessing people's strengths/skills and assigning appropriate tasks, making scheduling decisions against a deadline, prioritising tasks based on requirements, assigning resources appropriately, and using a suitable software development lifecycle to organise tasks. A resource and cost plan identifying and costing materials, physical resources and personnel; allocating resources and attributing costs for an accurate total project cost estimate; assessing a project's affordability and viability over time. A rationale considering the most relevant planning factors and justifying notable decisions (task order/timing, team allocation, benefits/risks, impact on timings/costs). Task 2: Identifying and fixing defects in existing code Students assess given code against requirements, test it to identify issues, and perform remedial action, justifying their fixes. Documenting the testing process annotated evidence covering: tests to be carried out, the purpose of each test, test data used (valid, valid extreme, invalid, invalid extreme, erroneous), expected results, actual results, a comparison of the two, further actions needed, and refinement of the system. The solution correcting errors and adding/removing code so the given code is functional and meets requirements, following programming conventions so the logic and structure are precise and outcomes consistently correct. Task 3: Designing a solution Decomposition of the problem breaking the problem into computational parts, justifying decisions, using detailed abstraction/refinement, reusable components, and good decomposition to reveal every necessary sub system, communicated with appropriate tools (flowcharts, code). Application of logical thinking describing the solution's parts as algorithms with clearly and uniquely defined steps that depend on input and prior steps, using key constructs (sequence, selection, iteration). Use of conventions correct structure/convention for the chosen communication method (correct flowchart symbols, correct code keywords), with consistent naming conventions throughout. Communication of the design design documents detailed enough to communicate the intended solution, let the client make informed decisions, and let a third party build the proposed solution from them, using an appropriate mix of written/diagrammatic presentation, technical vocabulary, audience awareness, and explanations of structures/processes. Task 4a: Developing a solution The solution applying programming knowledge to build a solution meeting the brief's requirements: refining the system, demonstrating technical skill and problem solving, and using pre written/user written modules with an appropriate interface. Code organisation avoiding sprawling nested if clauses/loops with copy pasted code, using clear meaningful indentation, precise logic via functions/classes/objects with proper structure, comments to explain logic, mostly local variables with minimal global use, constants, a well designed interface, consistent style, defensive programming with secure data handling, and good exception handling. User experience consistency, simplified input, meaningful output/error messages, and data visualisation (e.g. using Matplotlib for graphs showing trends/patterns). Note: formal testing documentation isn't required for this task, but students should still test their work, evidenced implicitly through a working product that meets the brief. Task 4b: Reflective evaluation Applying reflection and evaluation techniques to provide evidence the product meets the brief: measuring against success criteria, evidencing from testing that it meets user needs, and discussing how it could be improved if revisited. What's assessed The Employer Set Project's Assessment Objectives (see Core scheme of assessment for the full weighting breakdown) cover planning, applying knowledge/skills to develop software and fix defects, selecting relevant tools/techniques/resources, English/maths/digital skills, and realising and reviewing a project outcome. Key terms Synoptic assessment assessment drawing together knowledge and skills from across the whole core component, rather than testing isolated topics. Decomposition breaking a problem or solution down into smaller, manageable parts. Defensive programming writing code that anticipates and safely handles unexpected inputs or conditions. title: Occupational Specialism Overview
text: Occupational Specialism Overview Digital Software Development T Level → Occupational Specialism Unlike some T Levels, Digital Software Development has only one occupational specialism also called Digital Software Development rather than a choice between several. Every student on this T Level studies the same specialism, worth 50% of the overall qualification alongside the shared Core Component. It prepares students for the specialist area of digital software development, building toward roles such as software developer/engineer within a wider development team (see Analyse a Problem, 1.2 for how that role fits alongside product owners, scrum masters, technical leads, UX/UI designers and testers). Designing, building and testing software solutions in at least two languages. The eight content areas 1. Analyse a Problem be able to analyse a problem to define requirements and acceptance criteria aligned to user needs. 2. Ethics and Risk apply ethical principles and manage risks in line with legal and regulatory requirements when developing software. 3. Sources of Knowledge discover, evaluate and apply reliable sources of knowledge. 4. Design understand and apply common design approaches, platforms and principles to design a software solution. 5. Create solutions in a social and collaborative environment working effectively as part of a development team. 6. Implement a solution using at least two appropriate languages building working software. 7. Testing a software solution planning and carrying out testing. 8. Change, maintain and support software looking after software once it's live. Content areas 1 4 are covered on this site's pages linked above; content areas 5 8 and the Scheme of Assessment are covered on their own pages, linked below. title: Analyse a Problem
text: Analyse a Problem Digital Software Development T Level → Occupational Specialism → Analyse a Problem This is Content Area 1 of the Digital Software Development occupational specialism: being able to analyse a problem to define requirements and acceptance criteria aligned to user needs. It walks through the whole software development lifecycle (SDLC), stage by stage, and covers the roles on a development team and the project methodologies used to plan and run software projects. 1.1 The software development lifecycle The SDLC is a structured set of stages a digital project moves through, from first idea to ongoing maintenance: Research and familiarisation understand the client's request/project brief, research the market and context (common problems/risks, current hardware/software use, emerging tech, existing solutions and how they meet user needs, industry regulations), and identify gaps in your own skills/knowledge so you can plan to fill them. Planning and requirement analysis explore the brief and define the scope of a solution as a project proposal: identify business requirements (new software, added security, etc.), assess the proposed solution's value to the user and the client/business, apply computational thinking (decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction) to break the problem into discrete parts, define functional and non functional requirements, set key performance indicators (KPIs), identify performance constraints, write user acceptance criteria, schedule the project (tasks, subtasks, milestones), allocate resources, estimate costs, choose a programming language (weighing suitability, organisational policy, scalability, security, staff availability, cost, reliability), and identify risks and how to mitigate them. Performing a user analysis use business analysis models to understand users and problems: user stories, activity diagrams, mind maps, product road maps, process diagrams, entity relationship diagrams. Designing the product create interface designs, plan algorithms to solve key problems, create data requirements designs, and use generative AI tools to help produce sections of code, reviewing and refining the AI output to make sure it actually meets requirements. Developing and testing the product build a prototype, then plan and run appropriate testing: module testing, system integration testing, automated testing, and user testing/feedback. Deploying/implementing the product install and configure it, update it, document key changes/iterations, and keep proper version control. Maintenance provide system and user support, fix bugs, arrange/carry out user training, and release updates that enhance the product. Students also need to understand the value the digital product brings to the organisation, and the role the SDLC plays in delivering that value. (Signposted competencies: E1 E5, M2, M6 M10, D1 D4.) 1.2 Roles and responsibilities in the digital team Product owner/client sets and communicates the product's requirements. Scrum master keeps the team cohesive and makes sure they have the resources they need. Technical lead provides technical guidance and support for the project team. Project manager plans, organises and manages every phase of a project (budget, scope, schedule, risk, quality). Software development team : systems analyst (analyses the current system, writes requirements, designs the new solution), UX/UI designer (interviews users, researches the market, designs the interface), software developer/engineer (builds and maintains a usable, secure, stable solution from the designs), operations engineer (keeps the product stable), security engineer (keeps the product secure). Software testers responsible for quality assurance across the software and the development process. (E4, E5.) 1.3 Project methodologies Students need to understand the key features of each methodology and be able to select the right one for a given project: Agile incremental delivery (sprint, epic, story, spike), high quality products with initially limited functionality, each increment adds functionality, requirements can keep changing, can lack formal documentation, users see working products every iteration, cost effective route to an initial market product, and even a cancelled project usually leaves some usable code. Scaled Agile Agile's incremental model expanded to include product increments, with cohesive reporting across larger teams, and a final iteration focused on stability. Waterfall rigid, systematic steps; progress measured by artefacts completed; high upfront cost with a slower return on investment; a project cancelled early may leave nothing usable; limited user/client interaction; heavy emphasis on documentation. Rapid Application Development (RAD) fast prototyping that's systematically improved; features come before quality; users may only see partial/mock up products early on; relies heavily on reusing existing code; best for small to medium projects. Lean focused on cutting "waste" (unnecessary features, repeated tasks, over complex solutions, poor communication, unnecessary changes); decisions deferred to the last responsible moment; short, fast iteration cycles; prioritises iterations that are fit for use over delivering every feature; suited to small teams with limited resources. User Centred Design (UCD) considers who the user is, what they want to achieve, how/when/why they interact with the product, and their overall experience; characterised as empathetic, iterative and interdisciplinary; follows an iterative cycle of understanding the context, specifying requirements, designing the solution, and assessing it against requirements. (E5, D1, D3, D6.) 1.4 Functional and non functional requirements Secure by design security is built into a decision from the start, shaping both functional and non functional requirements. Functional requirements define: the inputs needed, the data needed, the data processing that must happen, the system's logic, and the platforms the software will run on. Non functional requirements define: security considerations, required accessibility features, scalability, KPIs/metrics for responsiveness/load handling/reliability, and user acceptance criteria. Spike testing an early testing technique used to establish requirements and work out the scope of a problem and the solution needed. (E1, E5, M2, M6 M8, D2, D3, D6.) 1.5 Emerging technologies Students investigate how emerging technologies are affecting software development and industry more broadly, including: operational technology (OT); artificial intelligence (AI) and virtual intelligence (VI) and their subsets (conversational/generative AI, machine learning, object recognition, computer vision); the Internet of Things (IoT); biometrics; robotics and automation; cloud services and platforms; data lakes and data warehousing; drones; 3D printing; and developments in communications networks (e.g. 5G, wider broadband availability). (E1 E4.) 1.6 Identifying and addressing training needs To make sure they can actually deliver a solution, developers need to be able to: identify what further knowledge and skills they need, and judge whether they're currently able to complete the required work. They can then address gaps by: coaching from a professional or peer, learning on the job, self study, using professional online forums, or signing up to online workshops. (E5, E6, D1, D3, D6.) Key terms SDLC (Software Development Lifecycle) the structured stages a digital project moves through, from research to maintenance. KPI key performance indicator, a measurable target used to judge a solution's success. Functional requirement what a system must do (inputs, data, processing, logic, platform). Non functional requirement how well a system must do it (security, accessibility, scalability, performance). Spike testing early testing used to establish requirements and scope before full development. Agile / Waterfall / RAD / Lean project methodologies, each with different trade offs between speed, documentation, flexibility and team size. title: Ethics and Risk
text: Ethics and Risk Digital Software Development T Level → Occupational Specialism → Ethics and Risk This is Content Area 2 of the Digital Software Development occupational specialism: applying ethical principles and managing risk in line with legal and regulatory requirements when developing software. 2.1 Legal and regulatory requirements Students investigate and apply the legal and regulatory considerations relevant to the context they're developing software in, including: intellectual property rights and licences, consumer protection, age ratings and classifications, advertising laws, data protection and privacy, copyright and patent law, gambling legislation, staff/employment responsibilities, territorial restrictions, system security, and equality and diversity. They also investigate and apply relevant development standards, such as ISO/IEC/IEEE 90003:2018 (software engineering guidance) and W3C (web standards). Alongside the legal side, students consider the ethical implications of software development: code of conduct, professional practice, software licensing, and inclusion and diversity. (Signposted competencies: E5, M4 M6, D1, D5, D6.) 2.2 Identifying and managing risk Students assess the risks of developing a software product in its specific context and market: Risk identification covers: data/system security (malicious vs. accidental damage), compatibility with other systems, speed of development, meeting functional and non functional requirements, meeting KPIs, legal and ethical considerations, user engagement, and product reach. Risk assessment weighs likelihood against seriousness, and considers the risk's potential impact. Students then identify ways to mitigate each risk, build contingency plans , and set up ongoing monitoring . They also investigate the policies and procedures organisations use to manage and mitigate risk: backup, security, confidentiality/integrity/availability ( CIA ), personnel/skills/training, business continuity planning, and disaster recovery planning. Finally, students need to be able to make and justify software development decisions and recommendations, based on properly weighing risk against reward for the specific context and market they're working in. (E5, M4 M6, D1, D5, D6.) Key terms CIA confidentiality, integrity and availability, the three core properties an information security policy protects. ISO/IEC/IEEE 90003:2018 a standard giving guidance on applying software engineering practice. Business continuity planning planning to keep critical operations running during and after a disruptive incident. Disaster recovery planning planning to recover and restore systems/data after a disruptive incident. Contingency plan a predefined backup plan for when a risk materialises. title: Sources of Knowledge
text: Sources of Knowledge Digital Software Development T Level → Occupational Specialism → Sources of Knowledge This is Content Area 3 of the Digital Software Development occupational specialism: discovering, evaluating and applying reliable sources of knowledge both for research generally, and for gathering feedback to evaluate a software solution. 3.1 Evaluating the reliability of sources Students use a range of sources to find information: search engines to locate reliable websites, wikis, blogs, academic papers, conversations with peers, forums, code comments, and code repositories. To judge how reliable a source actually is, students evaluate: Reputation who wrote it, and are they credible? Bias was it written by a particular individual or organisation with an angle? Evidence what evidence backs up the content? Cross referencing/triangulation does it agree with other independent sources? Currency how up to date is it (when was it last updated)? (Signposted competencies: E1, E4 E6, M2, M4, M6 M8, D1, D3 D6.) 3.2 Gathering data to evaluate a software solution Students select and use a mix of qualitative and quantitative techniques to evaluate how well a software solution is working: Verbal feedback (formal and informal). Surveys and questionnaires. Performance and usage data. User observation, with observation records. Focus groups representing a cross section of the target audience. Interviews, to gather individual users' thoughts on the solution. Peer mentoring. Formal line management and appraisal procedures. (E1, E4 E6, M2, M4, M6 M8, D1, D3 D6.) Key terms Triangulation cross checking a claim against multiple independent sources before trusting it. Qualitative data descriptive, non numeric data (e.g. interview feedback, opinions). Quantitative data numeric, measurable data (e.g. performance/usage statistics). Focus group a small, representative group of target users consulted together for feedback. title: Design
text: Design Digital Software Development T Level → Occupational Specialism → Design This is Content Area 4 of the Digital Software Development occupational specialism: understanding common design approaches, choosing the right platforms for source code and content management, and designing a software solution end to end from UX/UI principles through to database and network design. 4.1 Common design approaches Students use critical thinking to pick the right design approach for a project, and apply it within the wider project methodology: Function oriented (top down) design focuses on how data flows through the system; the system is broken into sub systems (functions); data flow diagrams show how each function handles or changes data; the problem is logically divided based on what each function should do ("divide and conquer"). Object oriented programming (OOP) design makes code reusable through standard OOP structures (methods, classes, objects/instances); characterised by encapsulation, data abstraction, polymorphism and inheritance; uses common OOP design patterns (creational, structural, behavioural). Data model design visualises what data is needed and how it's organised, using common data models (conceptual, logical, physical, hierarchical, relational) and tools such as the Entity Relationship Model (E R Model) and Unified Modelling Language (UML). Test driven development (TDD) every new feature starts with a test that defines what the feature should do; the cycle is: add a test, run all tests until the new one fails, write the code, run tests and refactor, repeat. Behaviour driven development (BDD) development is driven by the required behaviour of a software unit, specified before coding starts; desired behaviours must have business value and map to specified requirements; behaviour specifications typically follow a title/narrative/acceptance criteria structure. Functional design the program is structured as a set of modules, each performing one defined process/function; characterised by recursion, closures, first class functions, higher order functions, anonymous functions and currying; built from arguments, statements, blocks, procedures and functions/sub routines. (Signposted competencies: E1 E5, M1 M8, M10, D1, D2, D4, D6.) 4.2 Platforms for source code and content management Students need to understand the features of development platforms at each stage: coding, repositories, branching, building, testing, deployment. This includes understanding: The differences between proprietary and open source platforms, and how that choice affects design. Development workflow management approaches ( GitFlow , GitHubFlow ). How to weigh up different platforms and make an informed choice based on: target audience, budget, technical features, staff and training, ease/speed of development, platform updates, security, reliability, performance, and compatibility. (E1, E3, E5, M10, D1 D6.) 4.3 Designing a software solution UX design principles : consistency (intuitive, aesthetically pleasing, on brand), information hierarchy (easier navigation), visual hierarchy (important content stands out), confirmation (users know what actions they've taken and their impact), user control (efficient navigation, workflow and error correction), and accessibility (works for a wide range of users). UI design principles : wireframes, style guides, clickable prototypes. Content management system (CMS) features : SEO, page/screen management, social media integration, analytics tools, workflow management, publishing controls, security features, versioning and rollback, content repositories, open APIs, multilingual support, and general support. Program design conventions : pre defined code, flowcharts using standard BCS symbols, pseudocode using standard notation, control structures (sequence, selection/branching, iteration), data types, data validation, and data structures. Selecting assets (graphics, audio, video, code): considering file types, file size, compression, streaming/encoding audio and video, metadata use, required quality, available bandwidth/storage, and the target platform. Working legally and ethically when using AI to generate content or assets for a software solution. Target platforms and how they shape design/development: operating systems, file systems, server/infrastructure (physical and virtual), the programming language stack, and mobile vs. web. Using databases to support a solution: user management, e commerce tasks (stock, order processing, page personalisation), diagnostics, and performance analysis. Database designs are created using a data dictionary/library, an entity relationship diagram (ERD), and normalisation to third normal form. Network integration points : which data is processed locally (e.g. user input in a game) vs. remotely (e.g. actions of all players in a multiplayer game), how data moves between local and remote sources (e.g. remote system calls), how local and remote systems connect, where the system boundaries sit, and which external systems to integrate with (e.g. a sports data feed). (E1 E5, M1 M8, M10, D1 D4, D6.) Key terms OOP (Object Oriented Programming) a design approach built on classes, objects, encapsulation, abstraction, polymorphism and inheritance. TDD / BDD test driven / behaviour driven development, where tests or required behaviours are defined before the code that satisfies them. ERD (Entity Relationship Diagram) a diagram showing how data entities relate to each other, used in data model and database design. Third normal form a level of database normalisation that reduces data redundancy and dependency issues. GitFlow / GitHubFlow structured branching workflows for managing code changes in a repository. title: Create Solutions in a Social and Collaborative Environment
text: Create Solutions in a Social and Collaborative Environment Digital Software Development T Level → Occupational Specialism → Social and Collaborative Environment This is Content Area 5 of the Digital Software Development occupational specialism. It's a short but important content area: it covers why and how development teams collaborate, and the tools that support that collaboration, rather than any single technical skill. 5.1 Reasons for using collaborative techniques Working as a team on a shared project, rather than solo, brings several benefits: A reduction in development time (work can happen in parallel). Better communication between everyone involved in the project. Sharing of knowledge across the team. Development of the team's overall software development skills. Code reviews, carried out through: paired programming informal walkthroughs formal inspections. Students also need to understand when it's better to collaborate versus when working independently is the more appropriate choice for a given task. (Signposted competencies: E5, M10, D1, D3.) 5.2 Selecting appropriate collaborative technologies Students should understand and be able to select the right technology to support teamwork, across several categories: Communication e.g. email, instant messaging. Resource management e.g. cloud storage, backup, synchronisation. Knowledge sharing collaboration hubs, wikis, community forums, news sites. Documentation for both technical and non technical audiences. On top of these general categories, students need to know about tools specific to software development teams: Code collaboration technologies. Version control tracking and managing changes to code over time. Source control specifically managing the source code itself as it's developed. Integrated development environments (IDEs) the software tools developers write and manage code in. (Signposted competencies: E5, M10, D1, D3, D6.) Key terms Paired programming two developers working together at one workstation, one writing code while the other reviews it in real time. Version control a system for tracking and managing changes to code and files over time (e.g. Git). IDE (Integrated Development Environment) software that bundles a code editor, debugger and other developer tools together. title: Implement a Solution Using at Least Two Appropriate Languages
text: Implement a Solution Using at Least Two Appropriate Languages Digital Software Development T Level → Occupational Specialism → Implementation This is Content Area 6, the core coding content area of the specialism. It covers choosing and using programming languages to build front end and back end solutions, building a working user interface, connecting code to data, and deploying the finished product. Students must select and use at least two languages for their software project. 6.1 Selecting and using languages appropriate to the project Students choose at least two appropriate languages from this list to build front end and back end solutions: Python 3 (version 3.10 or later) C SQL JavaScript PHP Tools, APIs, packages, modules and libraries. Students need to be able to select and use these to add functionality and compatibility, covering things like: generating dynamic page content containerisation stateful vs. stateless components form handling file and data handling (local files; create/open/read/write/delete/close files on a server; sending/receiving cookies; adding, deleting and modifying data in a database) interface components and media content adaptive/responsive layout working with existing applications, operating systems, cloud based and traditional platforms working with specific devices communication over a network infrastructure as code security features (controlling user access, encrypting data) Packaging the product. Students should be able to package and organise front end and back end code into a single usable product for example using HTML, CSS and related frameworks to deploy a solution, then compiling/encapsulating it as a single executable file. Continuous integration. Students need to understand what continuous integration continuous deployment (CI/CD) means, and the common stages of a CI/CD pipeline: source code control build automation unit test automation deployment automation monitoring Coding conventions. Students should use common coding conventions: naming conventions, code annotations/commenting, modularisation, structure/indentation, and version control. Good practice (the 12 factor principles). Students should apply good practice when developing digital products, based on the "12 factor app" principles: 1. Use one codebase tracked in revision control, with many deploys. 2. Explicitly declare and isolate dependencies. 3. Store configuration in the environment. 4. Treat backing services as attached resources. 5. Strictly separate build and run stages. 6. Execute the app as one or more stateless processes. 7. Export services via port binding. 8. Scale out via the process model. 9. Maximise robustness with fast startup and graceful shutdown. 10. Keep development, staging and production as similar as possible. 11. Treat logs as event streams. 12. Run admin/management tasks as one off processes. (Signposted competencies: E5, M1 M8, M10, D1 D4, D6.) 6.2 Selecting tools and features for a UX driven user interface User interface features. Students select and use appropriate features such as images and animation, audio, visual effects, and interactions (user input; output/feedback that can be textual, graphical, audio or haptic), plus data visualisation like dashboards, graphing and data presentation. User interface techniques. This covers layout grids, use of space, font selection and typesetting, letter spacing, line spacing, justification, use of colour and contrast, input focus, and hover controls. Design decisions. Students must weigh up: browser support, target device/platform, user characteristics, available bandwidth, style and branding, accessibility, and the user's input method (voice, text, touch screen, or mouse). (Signposted competencies: E5, M1, M4, M7, M8, M10, D1, D2, D6.) 6.3 Connecting code to data sources Students create data sources to support their software (using a database) and connect to them through different methods: API (Application Programming Interface) types of requests and request methods, endpoints, retrieving/parsing/displaying data, and API keys. JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) the core API, driver manager, connection statement, prepared statement, result set, and SQL queries. ODBC (Open Database Connectivity) the application, driver manager, driver, data source, and connection method (database name/data source, credentials, optional parameters). Once connected, students should be able to extract, store, update and delete data, and connect to network resources using tools within their development environment. Students must be able to select the data source and connection method that's actually appropriate to the context and market they're developing for, not just default to one approach. (Signposted competencies: E5, M4, M5, M6, M10, D1, D3, D4, D5, D6.) 6.4 Selecting deployment methods Students select and use deployment methods appropriate to the project, such as: local installation network/server installation mobile platforms web based platforms cloud based platforms containerisation container scheduling platforms (Signposted competencies: E5, M5, M6, M10, D1, D4, D6.) Key terms CI/CD continuous integration / continuous deployment; automating the build, test and release of software. 12 factor app a widely used set of principles for building software as a service apps that are portable and scalable. API Application Programming Interface, a defined way for one piece of software to request data/functionality from another. JDBC / ODBC standard interfaces for connecting an application to a database (JDBC for Java, ODBC as a more general cross platform standard). Containerisation packaging an application with everything it needs to run into an isolated, portable unit (e.g. Docker). title: Testing a Software Solution
text: Testing a Software Solution Digital Software Development T Level → Occupational Specialism → Testing This is Content Area 7. It covers the types of testing a software solution needs, the techniques used to carry it out, and how to design good tests and test data. 7.1 Functional, non functional and front end testing Students select and carry out the testing approach appropriate to the component being tested and the stage of the software development lifecycle it's at: Functional testing unit testing, smoke testing, integration testing, system testing. Non functional testing availability testing, compatibility testing, configuration testing, load testing. Front end testing checking code/script performance and functionality, browser compatibility, operating system compatibility, cross browser performance, formatting and rendering, loading times, and responsiveness. Security testing vulnerability scanning, static analysis, dynamic analysis, integration analysis. (Signposted competencies: E1, E4, E5, E6, M2, M4, M5, M6, M8, M10, D1, D2, D4, D6.) 7.2 Testing techniques Students select appropriate manual and automatic testing techniques (including the use of AI tools) to check a software solution meets its identified requirements: Acceptance testing does the software meet the client/user's requirements? Alpha testing early stage internal testing before release. Beta testing testing with a limited group of real, external users before full release. Closed box testing testing based only on inputs/outputs, without knowledge of the internal code (also called black box testing). Open box testing / structural testing testing based on knowledge of the internal code structure (also called white box testing). (Signposted competencies: E1, E4, E5, E6, M2, M4, M5, M6, M8, M10, D1, D2, D4, D6.) 7.3 Selecting tests and test data To test a piece of functionality properly, students need to define: The purpose of the test. The test data to use, across several categories: valid test data invalid test data valid extreme test data invalid extreme test data erroneous test data Any pre requisites the test depends on. The expected result . After running the test, the test plan should be updated with the actual results, any changes made as a result, and any re tests or regression testing carried out following those changes. (Signposted competencies: E1, E4, E5, E6, M2, M4, M5, M6, M8, M10, D1, D2, D4, D6.) Key terms Regression testing re running existing tests after a change, to make sure the change hasn't broken anything that used to work. Black box / white box testing testing based only on external behaviour (black box) versus testing informed by the internal code structure (white box). Extreme test data data right at the edge of what's valid or invalid, used to check boundary behaviour (e.g. the maximum allowed value, or one more than the maximum). Erroneous test data data that's the wrong type or format entirely, used to check the system fails safely rather than crashing.
