title: Change, Maintain and Support Software
text: Change, Maintain and Support Software Digital Software Development T Level → Occupational Specialism → Change, Maintain and Support This is Content Area 8, the final technical content area of the specialism. It covers why software needs to keep changing after release, how to manage that change process, how to maintain code as part of a team, and how to support the people who actually use the software. 8.1 Why digital products change Business driven development shapes the type of maintenance a product needs: Preventing identified and foreseeable issues e.g. changes to regulatory requirements, compatibility with new products/technology, changes in business process, or the release of a new product/service. Correcting unforeseen or previously unpreventable errors e.g. new "zero day" vulnerabilities caused by changes elsewhere in the system, a targeted attack, data corruption, or system failures. Iterating to keep the product relevant driven by user/client feedback, developments in technology, competition from other organisations, the need to improve efficiency, or the need to future proof the product. (Signposted competencies: E1, E2, E3, E5, D3, D6.) 8.2 The software change management process Managing a change properly involves several stages: 1. Identify the issues/changes coming out of the feedback or review process. 2. Document the developments and changes made to the project. 3. Communicate with different audiences (technical and non technical) about the change. 4. Plan the changes required. 5. Schedule the changes. 6. Carry out regression testing. 7. Control and release the updated product, whether the release is planned or reactive (e.g. an emergency fix). (Signposted competencies: E1, E2, E3, E5, M6, M10, D1, D3, D6.) 8.3 Maintaining code as part of a larger team Students need to understand and apply good coding principles when developing, adapting and maintaining code, working alongside other developers: Separating code and using modularity. Writing readable code. Using common/accepted coding conventions. Adding informative commenting/annotation within the code. Keeping change logs and other documentation up to date. (Signposted competencies: E1, E4, E5, E6, M2, M4, M5, M6, M8, M10, D1, D2, D3, D4, D6.) 8.4 Supporting software users Communicating with users. Students must be able to communicate with both technical and non technical audiences, using the right tone and level of technical vocabulary, through: face to face communication remote conferencing written formats: blogs, formal reports, technical documentation, release notes, user guides/help files, FAQs visual and audio formats: user demonstrations, screencast videos, narration (recorded voice or text to speech) machine readable API contracts Resolving issues. Students apply a systematic process to support users and resolve their issues: 1. Identify or replicate the issue. 2. Investigate the possible cause user error, system error, application error, or a security breach. 3. Apply testing techniques to identify the error in the system/code, make the necessary changes, confirm the error doesn't return, and confirm the fix hasn't caused any new issues. 4. Communicate how and when the issue was resolved to the appropriate stakeholders. 5. Document the lessons learned. (Signposted competencies: E1, E4, E5, E6, M2, M4, M5, M6, M8, M10, D1, D2, D3, D4, D6.) Key terms Zero day vulnerability a security flaw that's exploited before a fix exists for it. Regression testing re testing existing functionality after a change to make sure nothing that used to work has broken. Change log a running record of what's changed in a product and when, usually version by version. title: Occupational Specialism: Scheme of Assessment
text: Occupational Specialism: Scheme of Assessment Digital Software Development T Level → Occupational Specialism → Scheme of Assessment Unlike some T Levels, Digital Software Development has a single synoptic assessment for its one occupational specialism: one extended project, rather than a choice of several. The synoptic element matters because it's how students demonstrate threshold competence and provide evidence against every skill listed in the Performance Outcomes at once, rather than in isolated pieces. How the project is structured The project is externally assessed, runs for 50 hours 30 minutes in total, and is worth 144 marks . It's made up of several activities grouped into four substantive tasks: Task 1 : Analysing a problem and designing a solution. Task 2 : Developing the solution. Task 3a : Gathering feedback. Task 3b : Evaluating feedback. Each task runs during a window set by Pearson, during which providers schedule supervised assessment sessions; some tasks also allow unsupervised activity where that's genuinely needed for the skill being assessed. Students respond to a given scenario to complete the whole project, assessed on how they apply the skills listed under the Performance Outcomes below they are not assessed against separate "knowledge" outcomes, but are expected to draw on and apply that knowledge naturally while completing the tasks. Students work under a mix of supervised and controlled conditions, and internet access is permitted for every task except Task 3b. The finished project is a portfolio of evidence submitted electronically, and it's externally marked by Pearson. Use of AI. For Task 1 Activity C, students are expected to use a generative AI model (Pearson doesn't specify which, though a natural language model like ChatGPT or Google Gemini is suggested) to create short code snippets addressing a specific piece of functionality not to generate a single overarching solution to the whole brief. The chosen AI tool should let students show the specific prompts they used and review how well the output met the functionality it was meant to address. Performance Outcomes and weighting Performance Outcome Raw marks % of total marks PO1 Analyse a problem to define requirements and acceptance criteria, aligned to user needs 24 16.7% PO2 Design, implement and test software 57 39.6% PO3 Change, maintain and support software 18 12.5% PO4 Create solutions in a social and collaborative environment 9 6.3% PO5 Discover, evaluate and apply reliable sources of knowledge 18 12.5% PO6 Apply ethical principles and manage risks in line with legal and regulatory requirements when developing software 18 12.5% PO2 (design, implement and test) carries by far the most weight, at nearly 40% of the total reflecting that it's the core technical work of actually building the software solution. Grading The project is graded on the qualification's Occupational Specialism scale of Pass, Merit, Distinction or Unclassified , based on the total marks achieved against the 144 available. See Grading and Results for how this combines with the Core Component grade into an overall T Level grade. Delivery resources Providers need staff with relevant qualifications and/or experience in the digital sector, and a curriculum team whose combined knowledge spans the full breadth of the qualification content. General resources : software supporting Python 3.10+ and the other selected coding languages; word processing and spreadsheet software (e.g. MS Office); data back up solutions (external hard drives, network storage, cloud file stores); data encryption software (e.g. MS BitLocker); internet access; a printer. Specific resources : an IDE and debugger appropriate to the chosen languages; automated testing tools covering UI, performance, load/stress and compatibility testing; access to communication/collaboration/data collection tools including online code repositories (e.g. GitHub), forums (e.g. Stack Overflow), and questionnaire/survey tools (e.g. Google Forms, SurveyMonkey); access to AI code generation resources; access to online third party digital content (video/graphics); screencasting and video editing software; microphones and headphones. Key terms Synoptic assessment a single assessment that draws together and evidences skills from across the whole specialism, rather than testing each skill in isolation. Performance Outcome (PO) one of the six defined skill areas the project is marked against. Portfolio of evidence the electronically submitted collection of work produced across the project's tasks. title: Competency Frameworks and Command Words
text: Competency Frameworks and Command Words Digital Software Development T Level → Appendices → Competency Frameworks The specification signposts general English, maths and digital competencies against specific Occupational Specialism content, because that's where students get the most natural opportunity to develop them. These competencies are embedded in both the Core Component and the Occupational Specialism, using the short codes below (you'll see them referenced elsewhere in this guide, e.g. "E1, M6"). This page also lists the command word taxonomy used across Pearson's assessments for this qualification. General English competencies Code Students should be able to... E1 Convey technical information to different audiences E2 Present information and ideas E3 Create texts for different purposes and audiences E4 Summarise information/ideas E5 Synthesise information E6 Take part in/lead discussions General maths competencies Code Students should be able to... M1 Measure with precision M2 Estimate, calculate and spot errors M3 Work with proportion M4 Use rules and formulae M5 Process data M6 Understand data and risk M7 Interpret and represent with mathematical diagrams M8 Communicate using mathematics M9 Cost a project M10 Optimise work processes General digital competencies Code Students should be able to... D1 Use digital technology and media effectively D2 Design, create and edit documents and digital media D3 Communicate and collaborate D4 Process and analyse numerical data D5 Be safe and responsible online D6 Code and program Command word taxonomy This table shows the command words used consistently across Pearson's assessments for this qualification, so students know exactly what kind of response each word expects. Not every paper uses every word this list is for guidance. Command word What it requires Give / State / Name Provide a response (e.g. a feature, characteristic, use, or justification for something). Identify Select the correct answer from the given context or stimulus. Write Write code using information from the given context or stimulus. Describe Provide responses linked in an appropriate logical order. Explain Identify a point and give a linked justification of that point. Explain with additional justification Identify a point, give a linked justification, then a third point that further justifies the first justification. Discuss Consider the factors that apply to a specific context, giving careful consideration to opposing aspects of an issue, situation or problem. No conclusion required. Evaluate Consider various aspects of a subject's qualities relative to its context (strengths/weaknesses, advantages/disadvantages), reaching an evidence supported judgement, usually as a conclusion. Draw Produce a diagram (e.g. an algorithm, a process flow) using information from a given context or scenario. Complete Provide the missing information for a diagram so it's complete. Key terms Competency framework the shared set of English, maths and digital skills every T Level embeds and signposts against relevant content. Command word the specific verb an exam question uses (e.g. "evaluate", "describe") that tells you exactly what kind of answer is expected. Related pages What are T Levels? title: Flowchart Symbols and Python Command Reference
text: Flowchart Symbols and Python Command Reference Digital Software Development T Level → Appendices → Flowchart Symbols and Python Commands This appendix gives extra detail on two things students are expected to know throughout the Core and Occupational Specialism content: the flowchart notation used to express algorithms, and a reference list of Python commands and libraries. Students may explore Python in more depth than shown here if they choose it as one of their two implementation languages for the Occupational Specialism (see Implementation). This page is a guide and reference, not a replacement for the specification itself. Python command reference A working list of the Python built ins, keywords and library functions students are expected to know, grouped by purpose. Input, output, type conversions input() · print() · int() · str() · float() · bool() Selection if · elif · else · match case · try except Iteration while · for Functions def Standard libraries import math : math.floor(), math.ceil(), math.trunc(), math.sqrt(), math.pow(), math.pi random : random.random(), random.randint(), random.uniform(), random.sample() Built in functions range() · round() · max() · min() · count() · chr() · ord() · len() String handling isupper() · islower() · upper() · lower() · isalpha() · split() · len() · find() · index() · isalnum() · isdigit() · replace() · strip() · format() · concatenation using + Data structures (lists, arrays, dictionaries) index() · append() · insert() · remove() · count() · pop() · sort() · in · not in · len() Text files open() · write() · close() · read() · readline() · readlines() · line.strip() · line.split() Working with times and dates datetime.now() · strftime() · strptime() Additional libraries (Employer Set Project) For Employer Set Project questions, students also need a working knowledge of two data focused libraries: pandas Used to perform data analysis on a given .csv file. Students should be able to: import data from a provided .csv file; create and manipulate data frames using all or part of the imported data, as required; perform mathematical operations and statistical analysis on a data frame (or associated variable) e.g. identifying trends/patterns over time, calculating a total or average from a range of data, or counting occurrences of a specific item of data. Matplotlib Used alongside pandas to format and output data as part of analysing a .csv file. Students should be able to: select data and output it to appropriate graphs that meet a brief's requirements; format graph outputs so they're meaningful and easy to use (axis labels, colour schemes, legends, etc.). Flowchart symbols Flowcharts are used throughout this qualification to express algorithms and processes. The standard symbols are: Symbol shape Meaning Rounded rectangle / terminator Denotes the start and end of an algorithm. Rectangle Denotes a process to be carried out. Rectangle with double struck sides Denotes a sub process. Diamond Denotes a decision to be made. Parallelogram Denotes input or output. Circle (connector) Denotes a connection to part of a flowchart that can't easily be linked with an unbroken flow arrow. Arrow Shows the logical flow of the program. Key terms Data frame a pandas structure for holding and manipulating tabular data imported from a file such as a .csv. Connector (flowchart) a symbol used to link two points on a flowchart when a direct arrow would be impractical (e.g. across a page break). title: Help: Using This Wiki
text: Help: Using This Wiki Digital Software Development T Level → Help This page explains how to get around the site how search works, how the sidebar and breadcrumbs work, and how the wiki relates to the file library in the GitHub repository. Searching Use the search box at the top of every page. It searches the title and full text of every page as you type, not just headings so searching for a specific term (e.g. "acceptance criteria", "unit testing", "Python") will surface any page that mentions it, even if it's not in the title. Matching words are highlighted in the results, and each result shows a short snippet of surrounding text plus its file path so you know exactly where it lives. The sidebar directory tree The panel on the left mirrors the content/ folder in the GitHub repository exactly same folders, same files, same order. Click a folder name to expand or collapse it; click a page name to open it. Whatever page you're currently reading is highlighted in the tree, and its parent folders are automatically expanded. On narrow/mobile screens, tap the & 9776; button in the top left to show or hide the sidebar. The breadcrumb and "Contents" box Above every article title is a breadcrumb showing the folder path to that page click any segment to jump to that folder. Longer articles also get an automatically generated Contents box under the introduction, listing every section on the page as a jump link. Categories At the bottom of each article you'll see a Categories line this shows which part of the qualification the page belongs to (e.g. Core Component, or the Occupational Specialism), and clicking a category takes you to that section's overview page. Files vs. website Everything on this site is generated directly from the markdown files in the repository's content/ folder, so the two are always in sync. If you'd rather read the raw files for example, to search across everything at once with your own tools, or to download the whole library you can browse content/ directly on GitHub instead. See the main README for a guided starting point. This isn't the official specification This wiki is an independent, unofficial study guide. It paraphrases and reorganises the real T Level specification to make revision easier, but it is not the exam board's own document, and it can contain mistakes or fall out of date. For anything that actually matters for your assessment, always check the official specification and your course provider. See Sources and Further Reading for more official links. Key terms Breadcrumb the folder path trail shown above an article, letting you jump back up to any parent folder. Contents box the auto generated list of a page's own section headings, shown near the top of longer articles. Category the section of the qualification a page belongs to, shown at the bottom of the article and in the folder tree. Related pages Developers Sources and Further Reading

title: Developers
text: Developers Digital Software Development T Level → Developers This page is for anyone who wants to know how the site is built, contribute a fix or a new page, or get in touch with the person maintaining it. About this project This is an independent study guide project built and maintained by Samuel O'Connell , part of the UTC Leeds T Level Study Guides family. GitHub: github.com/lana6478 Email: samueloconnell62@gmail.com Source code: github.com/lana6478/T level Digital Software Development Found a mistake, an out of date detail, or want a topic covered in more depth? Open an issue on GitHub, or email directly both are welcome. How the site is built The whole project is two things living in one repository: content/ the actual study guide library: plain markdown files, organised into folders by topic. docs/ a small, dependency free static website (plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, plus marked.js for rendering markdown in the browser) built for GitHub Pages. It reads its page list and page content from docs/content/, a generated mirror of content/ so the website always shows exactly what's in the file library. There's no build framework, no bundler, and no server side code. Rebuilding the site after an edit After adding, editing or removing anything under content/ (or assets/), regenerate the site data from the repository root: This copies every file from content/ into docs/content/, copies shared images from assets/img/ into docs/assets/img/, and rebuilds docs/assets/data/manifest.json (sidebar tree) and docs/assets/data/search index.json (search index). Then preview it locally: Contributing a page 1. Add a new .md file under the right content/ subfolder, following the existing page template: an H1 title, an italic breadcrumb line, sections, a closing Key terms list, and a Related pages list of relative links to nearby pages. 2. Keep filenames lowercase and hyphenated, with a number prefix (01 , 02 , ...) where order matters. 3. Run python3 tools/build site.py so the website picks up the change. 4. Open a pull request. License and content note This project paraphrases and reorganises the official T Level Technical Qualification in Digital Software Development specification (Pearson, v1.1, August 2026) for easier navigation. It is unofficial and unaffiliated with Pearson or the Institute for Apprenticeships and Technical Education (IfATE). See Sources and Further Reading for the primary, authoritative documents. Key terms content/ the canonical markdown study guide library. docs/ the generated GitHub Pages website that reads from content/. tools/build site.py the script that mirrors content/ into docs/content/ and rebuilds the site's directory tree and search index.
